seoDescription: Learn how to craft a beautiful and unique piece of jewelry in this detailed tutorial. Follow the step-by-step process of making a silver ring with a Hawaiian koa wood overlay and a vibrant blue opal inlay. This guide covers key silversmithing techniques, including calculating ring size, soldering a sterling silver band, and pre-finishing. Discover the bent wood method for creating a strong, multi-layered wood exterior and see how to manually carve a channel and set a stunning opal inlay using a three-stage process.

chapters.title: Introduction & Project Overview
chapters.description: An introduction to the project of making a silver, koa wood, and blue opal ring, along with a sponsorship message.

chapters.title: Preparing the Silver Ring Blank
chapters.description: This chapter covers the calculation, cutting, and shaping of the sterling silver strip to prepare it for soldering.

chapters.title: Soldering the Sterling Silver Band
chapters.description: A detailed walkthrough of the soldering process used to join the silver ring band into a solid loop.

chapters.title: Shaping and Pre-Finishing the Silver
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to hammer the ring round, clean it, and then file and sand it to the correct width and a smooth pre-finish.

chapters.title: Creating the Bent Wood Overlay
chapters.description: Learn the bent wood method by preparing a strip of Hawaiian Koa wood, soaking it, and training it into a ring shape.

chapters.title: Gluing the Wood to the Ring
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to carefully glue the prepared bent Koa wood strips onto the silver ring core using cyanoacrylate.

chapters.title: Carving the Inlay Channel by Hand
chapters.description: A channel for the opal inlay is meticulously carved into the Koa wood overlay by hand using a marking gauge, file, and craft knife.

chapters.title: Setting the Blue Opal Inlay
chapters.description: This chapter details the three-stage process of filling the channel with crushed blue opal dust and larger chunks mixed with glue.

chapters.title: Applying the CA Glue Finish
chapters.description: The wood and opal are sealed and protected with multiple layers of cyanoacrylate (CA) glue to create a durable, glossy finish.

chapters.title: Final Polishing and Reveal
chapters.description: The final steps involve polishing the CA finish and the silver interior to a high shine before the finished ring is revealed.

summary:
## Ring Components & Materials
*   **Core:** 925 Sterling Silver
*   **Overlay:** Hawaiian Koa Wood (veneer)
*   **Inlay:** Crushed Blue Opal and blue pigment
*   **Adhesive & Finish:** Cyanoacrylate (CA) Glue / Superglue

## Creating the Silver Ring Band
1.  **Calculate Length:** The required length of the silver strip is calculated using the formula: `(inner diameter + silver thickness) * 3.14 (π)`.
2.  **Shape & Prepare:** The strip is cut, filed, and bent into a rough circle. The seam is perfected by running a saw blade through the join to ensure a tight fit.
3.  **Solder the Seam:** The ring is soldered closed using a blowtorch.
    > [!IMPORTANT]
    > The soldering process involves cleaning the ring in **pickle**, applying **flux** to the seam, placing small pieces of **silver solder**, and heating the entire ring evenly before focusing the flame on the seam until the solder flows.

## The Bent Wood Method
This technique creates a strong, layered wood exterior around the silver core.
*   A thin strip of Koa wood is cut.
*   One end is sanded to be paper-thin for a seamless overlap.
*   The wood is soaked in cold water for ~20 minutes to make it pliable.
*   The wet wood is wrapped tightly around a form (or the ring itself), secured with tape, and left to dry, effectively training it into a permanent ring shape.
*   The dried wood is then glued to the silver core in multiple layers using CA glue.

## Creating the Opal Inlay
*   **Carve the Channel:** An inlay channel is carved into the wooden overlay. This was done by hand using a **marking gauge**, a **triangle file**, and a **craft knife**.
*   **Three-Stage Inlay Process:** The inlay is built up in layers for a deep, complex look.
    1.  **Base Layer:** The channel is filled with a mix of fine opal dust, pigment, and CA glue.
    2.  **Main Layer:** Larger chunks of opal are pressed into a fresh layer of glue.
    3.  **Top Layer:** A final application of the fine dust mixture fills any remaining gaps.

## Finishing and Polishing
*   **CA Finish:** The wood and inlay are protected with a durable, waterproof, and glossy CA glue finish.
    > [!TIP]
    > Apply multiple (e.g., eight) thin layers of CA glue. Use an **activator spray** between coats to cure the glue instantly and build up the finish quickly.
*   **Sanding & Polishing:**
    *   The CA glue exterior is sanded smooth with progressively finer grits (up to 12,000) and polished with **burnishing cream** for a glass-like shine.
    *   The sterling silver interior is polished using **Tripoli** and **Rouge** polishing compounds with a rotary tool to achieve a mirror finish.
transcription:
## Introduction & Project Overview

Hey, what's happening guys? Welcome back to the workshop. In today's video, I'm going to show you how to make one of these silver rings with Hawaiian koa wood and a blue opal inlay. This was a hell of a nice piece of jewelry to make so if you like it, then give it a thumbs up and leave me comments with any questions and I'll do my best to answer them. And of course, if you want to help out the channel, then please subscribe and ring that bell for notifications.

Another way you can help the channel out is by checking out Skillshare.com. So Skillshare is a website where you get access to like over 20,000 classes online, and they range from everything from graphic design to creative business kind of stuff. And I've actually been taking a lot of classes recently on photography and silversmithing. So if you want to check that out, then you can get two months for free. So you have absolutely nothing to lose and then after that, it goes up about $15 per month. So check out Skillshare, use the link in the description, and you will get two months absolutely free, where you can take as many classes as you like. Just get on with the video, bro.

## Preparing the Silver Ring Blank

This ring started life as a strip of 925 sterling silver, and the first thing to do was some maths. So to figure out exactly how much silver I needed to cut, I did this equation where you take the inner diameter of the desired size, add the thickness of the silver, and then times that by 3.14, which is Pi, and that gave me 65.186 millimeters.

The next thing I did was scored a line on my silver with a caliper, and I used a jewelry saw to cut out my strip of silver.

Next thing to do was to prepare the ring for soldering. So I took a file and filed down both of the edges I just cut, and then used the pliers, a half round nose pliers to be exact, to get the ring into a rough shape ready for soldering. So I just kind of made it so that both of those edges would fit together in a rough ring shape. And then so that the seam would fit together nicely, I just ran a saw blade right down the middle of the seam, and that left me with a nice old blank ready for soldering.

## Soldering the Sterling Silver Band

Soldering is the most fun part of the process. Basically, before I began this, I bathed it in a pickle solution and then neutralized the pickle with baking soda. And then all I did was applied a bit of soldering flux and a few tiny bits of easy silver solder onto the seam, and then I just attacked it with a blowtorch. I heated the ring up evenly and then saw the flux kind of froth up. And then after the flux froths, it kind of melts down into like a puddle, and that's the point when you start to kind of focus the flame onto the seam. And then you'll see all the solder melt down into a puddle, and hopefully if you get it right, it runs down into the seam and forms a really nice solder joint.

## Shaping and Pre-Finishing the Silver

So after that solder flowed nicely, I just let the ring cool down. Then I hammered it out to a rough ring shape with a rawhide hammer on a metal mandrel, just so it's going to bring it to look like a ring instead of a melted piece of metal. Hammered it out and then pickled it for probably about half an hour to an hour. And then I was left with this, which is quite a nice-looking little silver ring blank.

The next thing to do was to clean that up to make it look a bit more presentable. So I used a few grits of sandpaper on my bench and then used some files and some filing to bring it to a nice pre-finish. And then because this ring was meant to be an 8 mil wide, I used a caliper to score a line so that it was marked at 8 mil, obviously. Then I took my saw and sawed off the excess. So I found the best way to do this was actually to like put it onto the mandrel and then use my bench peg to saw that down.

And then I just moved on to pre-finishing basically. So I took a few grits of sandpaper, worked on the inside tapers, worked over the seam, made sure it was scratch-free, and eventually I was left with a really nice-looking silver ring blank, ready for me to wrap some wood around.

## Creating the Bent Wood Overlay

So to make the wooden portion of this ring, I had a beautiful piece of Hawaiian Koa wood, which is rare but really, really nice. So I cut a strip of that using just a craft knife and a metal ruler, and then I took one end of the strip and sanded that down so that it was as thin as paper.

Then when I'd done that, I just slowly dumped that bit of wood in some water, just cold water, left it there for probably about 20 minutes before taking it out. And then I wrapped the wood around, secured it with a bit of masking tape, and then just allowed that to dry so that it would like train the wood to stay in a round ring shape. In the trade, they call this the bent wood method, and it basically makes like a super-strong wooden ring. After allowing that wood to dry for a few hours, I test wrapped it around my silver ring, and then cut off the excess so that I was left with two layers of wood around the outside of the ring.

## Gluing the Wood to the Ring

Then I just started gluing it all together. So I used superglue, which is cyanoacrylate glue, and I basically worked my way around, like centimeter at a time, applying a little bit of glue to the wood, then sticking it down to the wood and ring until, like I said, two wrapped up layers of wood around my silver ring. And then just sanded off the edges on my bench with a bit of sandpaper, and I was left with this.

## Carving the Inlay Channel by Hand

Alright, what's next? Inlays. So I cut an inlay channel by marking a line with my marking gauge. And then I was sitting down and I was enjoying listening to an audiobook, so I actually cut the inlay for this one by hand with a triangle file. So I started with a triangle file. You could probably do this on the lathe, with a metal lathe, wood lathe, with a parting tool, whatever you want, but I was just enjoying my book so I wanted to sit down and enjoy it. And then I cut two other lines next to that and just used a sharp craft knife to carve out an inlay channel. There's probably people screaming at their screens right now going, 'Why don't you just put it on the lathe?' But honestly, I was totally engrossed and I just couldn't turn the book off. So yeah, anyway, I carved an inlay channel which was nice and deep.

## Setting the Blue Opal Inlay

And then I started working on my inlay. So for this inlay, I was given some opal by theopaldealer.com, The Opal Dealer on Instagram. Check them out, absolutely amazing materials. And I basically split this into larger chunks and dust, then mixed with a bit of blue pigment.

So what I started doing, I did it in three stages basically. The first stage was to fill the inlay channel with like the finer dust, just to give it like a bit of a base. So I put in a two globs of glue and then spooned some of that dust into there. And then for the second stage, I inlaid the larger bits. So just used the same technique, applied a bit of glue, and then pressed the ring into the big chunks of opal. I was left with that. And then for the third stage, I just went back over with the finer dust, just to fill in any gaps. So it was like a three-stage inlay.

My book was awesome the entire time. I was actually listening to I am Legend and it was amazing, couldn't turn it off. But yeah, there you go. This is the ring with the inlay, a bit messy obviously.

## Applying the CA Glue Finish

So the next thing to do was to clean that up, which I did with a diamond tip file on my lathe. And then I moved on to a few grits of sandpaper, took it up to like a 12,000 grit, and applied a bit of sanding sealer over the top to have a look what my finish was going to look like. And oh my God, look at those fires! Hell yeah.

I needed to protect the wood from the elements, so I used a CA finish, a cyanoacrylate finish, which is super glue. Lots of people use UV resins, which is absolutely fine, or there's probably epoxy resins that could do this or even just an oil finish. But I like CA glue. It's glassy, provides excellent protection, is durable, is waterproof, and I've just had lots of practice in applying it. So I just applied eight layers to every surface, like the edges and the front, the outside of the ring, and in between every coat I used an activator spray. And then I was left with this. So the outside of the ring was now coated in CA glue.

## Final Polishing and Reveal

And from there I just moved over to the final polishing stage. So to taper the inside edges of the silver ring and polish the outside of the CA, I just mounted the ring in some Chuck Jaws, pin jaws on the chuck, and sanded them there. And then I did the same thing on the outside on a spindle, and I just worked up to 1200 grit sandpaper before burnishing the outside with Chestnut Products Burnishing Cream. That left me with this super shiny, beautiful finish. So very impressed with it.

And then for the inside of the silver, I'd already sort of like sanded it up to a really high, kind of 2,000 grit. So I just took two polishing compounds, Tripoli and Rouge, and just worked those in with my rotary tool just to bring out a really beautiful shine in the silver.

And that's it. That's the finished ring on my dodgy turntable, which isn't straight at all. But I hope you enjoyed the video. Let me know what you think. If you have any questions, leave me a comment. Like I said, subscribe, help out the channel, and get your two months membership on Skillshare. So until I see you in the next one, go and check out some more of my videos. They should pop up on the screen. Click through and enjoy.
